newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban reinforce Islamic law in Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Taleban reinforce Islamic law in Afghanistan.

text.p: Afghanistan's new Taleban regime reinforced its command of Kabul on Friday, denouncing foreigners and standing by its strict Islamic law.

But a senior Iranian cleric accused the Taleban of defaming Islam by imposing "fossilised" policies and in Geneva the United Nations chief human rights official called on the Taleban to guarantee the rights of Afghan women to work and be educated.
The leaders of five former Soviet states also voiced concern at the Taleban's rise to power and said they would take steps to stop fighting spilling onto their territories.

Iran's Ayatollah Ahmad Jannati told worshippers at Tehran University: "Through their fossilised policies, they (Taleban) stop girls from attending school, stop women from working out of homes and all that in the name of Islam."
But a senior mullah from the Taleban defended the group's fundamentalist Islamic policies and accused outsiders and foreign media of waging a propaganda war against the country's new rulers.

In the first such sermon since the Taleban takeover a week ago, Syed Ghiasuddin, acting education minister, said human rights groups and foreign news agencies had been targetting the Taleban's imposition of a fundamentalist Islamic code.
"What we are doing is all based on Islamic Sharia law including amputating hands, executing and ordering people to the mosque five times a day," he said at Kabul's main mosque.

London-based human rights group Amnesty has accused the Taleban of seizing up to 1,000 prisoners in house-to-house searches in Kabul in what it called a reign of terror and said children and women were being ill-treated.

The Taleban entered the capital on September 27 after a lightning offensive chased out the forces of president Burhanuddin Rabbani. His forces and those of rival warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum remain holed up in separate areas north of the capital.
On Friday, dozens of educated, middle-class people were scrambling to leave Kabul at dawn, fleeing what one called a prison built by the purist Islamic Taleban militia.
"It's like being in jail. I want to be free," said one former ministry official as he boarded a minibus heading for the Pakistani border with his wife, son and two young daughters.
Few among those leaving for the eight-hour journey along a badly damaged road to the border were willing to talk as Taleban fighters wandered through the dusty bus station.
"They're looking for people who worked for the former government," said one man whose brother is an officer in the ethnic Tajik militia of former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.
Masood withdrew to his home base in the Panjsher Valley north of Kabul. The largely ethnic Pushtun Taleban have said they will attack him unless he surrenders.

The Taleban have issued decrees in the past week placing strict limitations on the activities of women, banning western dress, card-playing, music and television and vowing stern punishment for those found drinking alcohol, taking drugs or having illicit sexual relations.
Syed Ghiasuddin defended the restrictions on women, saying the female was like a flower to be nurtured at home.
"It is like having a flower, or a rose; you water it and keep it at home for yourself to look at it and smell it. It is not supposed to be taken out of the house to be smelled," he said.
Ahead of Friday prayers, the streets of the capital were quiet. Armed Taleban fighters lounged outside government departments while local people passed by warily.
But as prayers approached, witnesses said the area around the mosque became more tense as Taleban guards were seen hauling people from vehicles and nearby stalls to worship.
Crucial western aid to the country, one of the world's poorest, could end unless Kabul's new purist Islamist rulers change their attitude to women working, aid officials said.
"I think we all agree that we should do the winter programme at any cost because there is a highly vulnerable population facing severe weather with few resources," said one.

In Geneva, Jose Ayala-Lasso, U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, called publicly on Taleban supreme leader Mullah Mohammad Omar "to ensure respect for such rights as the right of women to work and the right of girls to education without discrimination" in line with past commitments by Afghanistan.

In the Kazakhstan capital Almaty, a summit meeting of five former Soviet states which also included Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and big regional power Russia denounced atrocities committed by Taleban militia after they seized Kabul.

Uzbek President Islam Karimov said that warlord Dostum was all that stood between the radical Taleban and former Soviet republics in Central Asia and he urged stronger support by the 12-member Commonwealth of Independent States for Dostum.

But there was no indication that the other CIS leaders shared his view. Kazakhstan's President Nursultan Nazarbayev made clear that the CIS would steer clear of involvement unless the conflict threatened the group's borders.
